title: Every swallow sets off a wave of muscle that squeezes food down to your stomach

cover.alt: A black-and-white X-ray of a chest, shown inverted, with a dark column of swallowed barium filling the lower part of the food pipe.

body: Food doesn't simply drop into your stomach. Swallowing starts **peristalsis**: rings of muscle in the [oesophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophagus) contract and relax in turn, a wave that squeezes the ball of food, or bolus, down a tube about 25 cm long. The first wave carries it into the stomach in about 8 to 9 seconds. If anything is left behind, a local reflex sends a second wave around it.

slides.alt: An inverted X-ray video of a chest: dark barium liquid runs down the food pipe, pools in its lower part, then is squeezed through a narrow neck into the stomach.
slides.caption: A barium swallow X-ray, shown inverted so the barium looks dark: the liquid fills the lower food pipe, then is squeezed through into the stomach.

steps.label: You swallow a bolus, a ball of food
The epiglottis folds over your airway
A muscle wave squeezes it down 25 cm
A ring of muscle helps keep acid down

slides.label: for the first squeezing wave to carry food into the stomach
slides.text: The upper third of the oesophagus is striated muscle, the type in your limbs, the lower third is smooth muscle, and the middle is a mix of both.

slides.question: In the large intestine, how often do the big 'mass' contractions that push its contents along happen?
slides.explanation: In the large intestine, peristalsis is not the main push. Instead, strong mass contractions happen one to three times a day.

slides.clue: The name for a wave of muscle squeezing along a tube, like the one that moves food through your gut
slides.detail: From the Greek peristellein, 'to wrap around'. Earthworms crawl by peristalsis too.
